newsitem.title: USA: British telecoms merger caps 28-year saga for MCI.
newsitem.headline: British telecoms merger caps 28-year saga for MCI.

text.p: The merger announced on Sunday between MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc caps a 28-year history of MCI's hammering at the long-distance market once dominated by AT&T Corp.

Founded by Bill McGowan in 1968 as MICOM, or Microwave Communications of America Inc, the company was the first to be authorised by the Federal Communications Commission to compete against AT&T in the domestic long-distance market.
MCI started offering point-to-point private-line service between Chicago and St. Louis in January, 1972, sold stock and was incorprated as MCI Communications in 1973.

The next decade was spent as a David challenging Goliath in the marketplace. The Washington, DC-based company filed an antitrust suit against AT&T in 1974. Six years later, a jury ruled in MCI's favour on almost all counts and awarded the company $1.8 billion.
But it was the 1982 decision by the U.S. Department of Justice and AT&T to break up the monopoly structure that radically changed MCI's prospects along with the telephone industry at large.

MCI said the AT&T divestiture led to the purchase of Western Union International Inc from Xerox Corp and a global expansion that made the comapny one of the "Big Three" long distance competitors alongside AT&T and Sprint Corp.
By 1988, the company said it had gained 10 percent of the total long-distance market share and more than doubled its revenue from $2 billion to about $5.1 billion.

MCI launched a series of new products and made a number of acquisitions and alliances in the early 1990s, including the launch of its Friends & Family savings plan and a $1 billion partnership with News Corp.
When founder McGowan died of a heart attack in 1992, the company named Bert Roberts to the chairman's post.

With the help of recent expansions into the Internet and wireless communications, MCI now has about 20 percent market share in the $75 billion U.S. long distance market and annual revenue of $15 billion.
In 1993, MCI and BT initiated a worldwide strategic alliance, with BT investing $4.3 billion in MCI and getting a 20 percent stake in the company.

The two companies started Concert, a joint venture that provides global communications services for multinational business customers, and BT and MCI are to use that name for their merged global company.
The merger announced on Sunday will mean the new enlarged Concert buying the remaining 80 percent of MCI.
